principles: Keep sentences short and concrete for readers aged 5 to 6.
Retain useful science vocabulary only when the surrounding sentence explains it.
Prefer factual clarity over catchy comparisons that can confuse the image sequence.

pages.reason: Names the Moon's relationship to Earth accurately and removes the vague neighbour wording.
pages.text: The Moon is a huge ball of rock. It travels around Earth. It takes about one month to go all the way around. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite.

pages.reason: Explains reflected light directly without implying that the Moon has an inner glow.
pages.text: The Moon does not make its own light. It does not glow by itself. The light we see is sunlight reflected from the Moon's surface.

pages.reason: Makes clear that the apparent shape changes gradually and uses looks rather than saying the Moon itself changes shape.
pages.text: The Moon's shape seems to change a little from night to night. Sometimes it looks like a full, bright circle. Sometimes it looks like a thin crescent. These shapes are called the phases of the Moon.

pages.reason: Replaces the misleading word holes with the concrete, level-appropriate word dents.
pages.text: The Moon's surface is covered in craters. Craters are bowl-shaped dents made when space rocks crashed into the Moon long ago. Some craters are bigger than cities.

pages.reason: Removes a shortened disputed quotation and gives a clear, accurate Apollo 11 sequence.
pages.text: In 1969, the Apollo 11 astronauts travelled to the Moon. Neil Armstrong became the first person to step onto its surface. Buzz Aldrin walked there soon after.

pages.reason: Acknowledges the Sun's smaller tidal effect while keeping the explanation concrete.
pages.text: The Moon's gravity is the main force behind Earth's tides. The Sun's gravity helps too. At high tide, the sea rises up the beach. At low tide, it moves back.

pages.reason: States more precisely what lunar samples reveal while reducing sentence complexity.
pages.text: Astronauts brought Moon rocks back to Earth. Scientists are still studying them today. The rocks tell us about the Moon's past and the early Solar System.

pages.reason: Replaces the sports-ball analogy with a direct and visually coherent size comparison.
pages.text: The Moon looks small from Earth, but it is very large. It is about one quarter as wide as Earth. About four Moons could fit across our planet.

pages.reason: Avoids claiming that the Moon is visible most nights or always visible while ending with a reassuring recap.
pages.text: You can see the Moon on many clear nights. With a telescope, you can see some craters. Even when you cannot see it, the Moon is still travelling around Earth.
